newsitem.title: USA: FERC aims to speed up utility merger approvals.
newsitem.headline: FERC aims to speed up utility merger approvals.

text.p: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Wednesday adopted new guidelines for reviewing electric utility mergers, looking to speed up approvals in a rapidly evolving market.

The guidelines, focusing on the impact of mergers on competition, rates, and regulation, have been long-awaited by the industry. Currently, there are pending unions worth an estimated $25 billion as utilities seek to gird themselves to compete in an open power market.

Nine merger applications are pending at the FERC, including Enron Corp. with Portland General Corp., Baltimore Gas and Electric Co. with Potomac Electric Power Co., IES Utilities with Wisconsin Power and Light, and Northern States Power Co. with Wisconsin Electric Power.
Under the new policy, a merger could be approved as quickly as five months after being filed.

"Mergers that protect existing customers from harm and are consistent with the policy goal of robust competition will be approved," Commissioner William Massey said at a FERC meeting. "Mergers that fail this test and cannot adequately be fixed through the imposition of pro-competitive provisions will be rejected."

Replacing a 30-year-old framework that often left applications languishing for two years or more, the commission said it was aiming to decide on all mergers within 12 to 15 months of receiving completed applications. But it made clear that the clock would be set back if applicants changed plans in midstream, as they had in the past.

The commission adopted the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission guidelines to screen mergers for their effects on competition. Those criteria include whether the merger would concentrate market power in the new company, whether there were barriers to others entering the market, whether efficiencies gained in the merger could be achieved any other way, and whether any of the companies would go under without the merger.

The commission said it would no longer weigh the costs and benefits of a takeover, which had been a major source of legal delays for mergers. It also would no longer look at accounting issues or whether any company had been forced into a merger.
It said it would focus on protecting ratepayers from sharp price increases, and encouraged companies to negotiate rates with their customers before filing a merger application.
If it found a merger would increase market concentration in a region or for a product, companies would have to take steps to offset that market power to win a merger approval.
Measures could include sale of power plants, building of new transmission lines or creation of an independent system operator to handle all electricity transmission.
Companies would have to take interim steps, such as foregoing certain power sales, if any of the proposed measures to limit their market power would take a long time to carry out.
Utilities and competing power producers hailed the new guidelines for potentially speeding up and providing more certainty in the merger approval process.

"By clarifying its position on electric industry mergers, the Commission has signalled its intent to prevent competitors in a restructured industry from eating into customer savings through the exertion of market power," said Steven Burton, chairman of the Electric Power Supply Association, which represents power producers.

Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities, applauded the commission for adopting the Justice Department's merger guidelines and for recognising that other factors, such as competitors' access to markets on newly open transmission lines, had to be taken into consideration to evaluate market power.
Commissioner Donald Santa said the new framework would be appropriate for reviewing unions between natural gas and electric companies, a new trend among utilities.
